results.result: Very mild head trauma (vmHT) delivered at different ages produces age-dependent acute sensorimotor deficits without affecting survival. D3Inj flies showed no acute climbing deficits, D17Inj females showed transient deficits at 90 min that recovered by 24 hr, while D31Inj flies of both sexes showed substantial and persistent deficits at both 90 min and 1 day post-injury.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C23 are well-supported by survival data (Figure 1B) and climbing index measurements (Figures 1D-F) with appropriate statistical analyses. The data clearly demonstrate age-dependent acute effects with proper controls and replication (n>50 for survival, n≥10 per video with 9 videos per condition).

results.result: vmHT does not cause acute structural brain damage or neuronal death at 1 day post-injury. No changes in vacuolation, mushroom body structure, or PDF neurons were observed, and TUNEL staining showed minimal signal comparable to sham controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C34 are supported by multiple imaging modalities (Figures 2A-C, Figure 2—figure supplements 1-2) with appropriate positive controls (eye-stabbing injury). The lack of acute structural damage is consistently demonstrated across multiple brain regions and injury ages (n>10 brains per condition).

results.result: vmHT causes late-life sensorimotor deficits that are sexually dimorphic and age-at-injury dependent when assessed on D45. Females show deficits across all injury ages, with D3Inj females being the only group affected in the youngest cohort, while males only show significant deficits when injured at D31.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C42 are well-supported by climbing index data (Figure 3A-B) with appropriate statistical analyses (repeated-measures ANOVA, n≥10 flies per trial, 9 videos per condition). The sexual dimorphism and age-dependency are clearly demonstrated with proper normalization to sham controls.

results.result: vmHT induces late-life brain vacuolation in a sexually dimorphic and age-dependent manner on D45. All female injury cohorts showed significant increases in vacuole number and area, while only D31Inj males showed significant vacuolation. Vacuoles were predominantly located in the neuropil, with D31Inj females showing a higher percentage of cortical vacuoles.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C45, C47-C48 are supported by quantitative imaging data (Figures 3C-F) with appropriate sample sizes (n>30 brains per condition) and statistical tests (Wilcoxon rank-sum tests). The spatial distribution analysis provides additional mechanistic insight.

results.result: Recovery time-matched analysis reveals that vmHT exposure early in life has minimal acute effects but causes neurodegenerative conditions at advanced ages, with aging accelerating the development of these conditions. Younger injury ages show smaller decreases in sensorimotor abilities within the same 2-week recovery period.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C55 are supported by recovery time-matched data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) comparing behavioral and pathological outcomes at 2 weeks post-injury across different age cohorts. The data demonstrate both age-matched and recovery time-matched effects with appropriate controls (n>12 brains, n>15 flies per condition).

results.result: AI-assisted tracking reveals that vmHT disrupts both movement speed and directional climbing in an age-dependent and sexually dimorphic manner. Females show progressively larger shifts to slower speeds from D3Inj to D31Inj, while males only show decreases in D17Inj and D31Inj. Both sexes show aberrant climbing angles, with females affected across all injury ages.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C61 are supported by detailed idtracker.ai analysis (Figure 4, Video 1) providing high temporal resolution (1/60 s) tracking of 15-20 individual flies. The speed and angular distribution analyses are quantitative and statistically validated (two-sample t-tests), though the arbitrary definition of 'normal' climbing angle (±30°) could be better justified.

results.result: Mating status, not body size, determines female vulnerability to injury-induced neurodegeneration. Virgin females, despite being similar in size to mated females, show no injury-induced climbing deficits or brain vacuolation on D45, and reducing injury force to match male impact levels does not eliminate deficits in mated females.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C68 are well-supported by comparative data between virgin and mated females (Figure 5) with appropriate controls for body size/mass differences. The reduced injury experiment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) directly tests the size hypothesis. Sample sizes are adequate (n>20-30 per condition) though the reduced injury experiment has only one replicate (n=15).

results.result: Sex peptide signaling through the reproductive pathway is responsible for female vulnerability to injury-induced neurodegeneration. Females mated to SP0 males, females with pan-neuronal SPR knockdown, and females with SPSN-specific SPR knockdown all show no injury-induced deficits in lifespan, climbing behavior, or brain pathology.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76 are strongly supported by genetic manipulation experiments (Figure 6A-C) using three independent approaches to disrupt SP signaling. All three methods produce consistent results with appropriate sample sizes (n>30 per condition). The convergence of evidence from multiple genetic interventions strongly supports the causal role of SP signaling.

results.result: Post-injury mating experiments demonstrate that SP signaling and vmHT pathways interact synergistically. Virgin females injured on D3 and then mated to wildtype males on D10 show reintroduction of injury-induced phenotypes on D45, while post-injury mating with SP0 males does not alter the virgin injury response.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79 are supported by temporal manipulation experiments (Figure 7) showing that SP exposure after injury can rescue the phenotype. The experimental design with appropriate controls (SP0 males) and adequate sample sizes (n>20-40 per condition) provides strong evidence for pathway interaction, though the mechanism remains to be elucidated.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis at 1 day post-injury reveals sexually dimorphic and reproductive status-dependent transcriptomic responses to vmHT. Males show 76 differentially expressed genes, wildtype-mated females show 121 changes, while virgin and SP0-mated females show minimal changes (16 and 13 respectively), with only 14 genes shared between males and wildtype-mated females.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C86 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 8B-D) with appropriate experimental design (n=40 brains per condition, 3 biological replicates). PCA and differential expression analyses are properly conducted using DESeq2. However, the small number of differentially expressed genes and lack of overlap between conditions raises questions about statistical power and biological significance.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis at 6 weeks post-injury reveals minimal transcriptomic changes that are sexually dimorphic and reproductive status-dependent. Males show 11 differentially expressed genes, wildtype-mated females show 8 changes, virgin females show 2 changes, and SP0-mated females show 20 changes, with minimal overlap between conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C92 are supported by chronic timepoint RNA-seq data (Figure 8E-F) with the same experimental design as the acute timepoint. The very small number of differentially expressed genes at the chronic timepoint is surprising given the robust behavioral and pathological phenotypes, suggesting either high variability, insufficient power, or that transcriptomic changes are not the primary driver of chronic phenotypes.

results.result: Seven unique genes are altered in wildtype-mated female brains at the chronic timepoint, including three immune-related genes (decreased Metchnikowin and Diptericin B, increased Prophenoloxidase 2). These genes were not identified at the acute timepoint, suggesting involvement in late-life neurodegeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C98 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 8F-G) identifying specific genes unique to wildtype-mated females. The immune-related genes are properly annotated with GO terms and citations. However, the inference that these genes are 'involved in' late-life neurodegeneration (C98) is speculative without functional validation. The correlation is clear but causation is not established.

results.result: The mild injury paradigm elicits a very small number of differentially expressed genes across all conditions and timepoints, likely due to the mild nature of the injury. No acute gene changes persist to the chronic timepoint, suggesting dynamic transcriptomic changes throughout the lifespan.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C116 are partially supported by the RNA-seq data showing few differentially expressed genes and no overlap between acute and chronic timepoints. However, C114 and C115 are speculative explanations without direct evidence. The lack of persistent gene changes could also reflect insufficient statistical power, high biological variability, or that the key molecular changes occur at intermediate timepoints not sampled.

results.result: At 6 weeks post-injury, vmHT overwhelmingly depresses AMP and AMP-like gene expression in male and mated female brains but not in virgin or SP0-mated females. This contrasts with previous findings of elevated AMP expression at earlier timepoints, suggesting temporally dynamic immune responses. The suppression of Metchnikowin and Diptericin and increased PPO2 correlates with female-specific late-life deficits.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C121 are supported by RNA-seq data showing decreased AMP gene expression at the chronic timepoint and citations to previous work (C118). The temporal dynamics are inferred by comparing current results to prior literature. However, the correlation between immune gene changes and behavioral/pathological phenotypes (C121) does not establish causation. Functional validation would be needed to confirm the mechanistic role.

results.result: The study establishes that mild head trauma in Drosophila causes late-life neurodegenerative conditions that disproportionately affect females, are exacerbated by increasing age-at-injury in a sexually dimorphic manner, and are mediated by sex peptide signaling and reduced innate immune defense transcripts in mated females.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C8 represent the main conclusions of the study and are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence including behavioral assays, brain pathology, genetic manipulations, and RNA-seq data. The causal relationship (C7) is supported by the temporal sequence of injury followed by late-life phenotypes and the genetic rescue experiments. However, 'causal' is a strong claim that would ideally be supported by additional mechanistic validation beyond correlation and genetic association.

results.result: Aging worsens post-head injury recovery and accelerates injury-induced neurodegeneration, consistent with findings in humans and other animal models. Older populations are at higher risk of developing negative consequences following mild head injury.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C25, C99-C102 are supported by the age-at-injury experiments showing progressively worse outcomes with increasing age. The consistency with human and other animal model data (C99-C100, C102) is supported by appropriate citations. The Drosophila data provide strong experimental evidence for the age-dependency of injury outcomes.

results.result: Sex differences in aging-associated vulnerability show that mated females exhibit a possible plateau effect between D17 and D31 injury, while males are very resilient at younger ages but show drastic acceleration of neurodegeneration when injured at D31, suggesting males show a larger decline in resistance to injury-induced neurodegeneration with age.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C109 are supported by the age-at-injury data (Figure 3) showing different trajectories for males and females. However, the 'plateau' interpretation (C106) and the claim that males show a 'larger decline' (C109) are somewhat subjective interpretations of the data. The data clearly show sex differences in age-dependency, but the specific characterizations could be quantified more rigorously.

results.result: The mechanism underlying female vulnerability involves mating-induced immunosuppression mediated by sex peptide signaling and Juvenile Hormone, which compounds injury-induced changes to disrupt immune homeostasis. This results in decreased AMP expression at advanced ages, making mated females unable to mount sufficient immune responses to pathological insults.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C129 are largely based on citations to previous literature (C122-C126) and speculative mechanistic interpretations (C127-C129) of the current RNA-seq data. While the model is plausible and consistent with the data, direct experimental evidence for the proposed mechanism (e.g., Juvenile Hormone involvement, immune homeostasis disruption) is not provided in this study. The correlation between immune gene suppression and phenotypes is clear, but causation is not established.

results.result: Acute sensorimotor deficits after vmHT are not caused by acute structural brain disruptions or neuronal death, and neuronal death is not the major contributor to vacuole formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C31, C34, C49 are supported by the lack of acute structural changes (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 1-2), minimal TUNEL staining, and the neuropil localization of vacuoles. However, these are inferences based on negative results. The actual mechanisms underlying acute deficits and vacuole formation remain unclear. Alternative mechanisms (e.g., synaptic dysfunction, glial changes) are not ruled out.

results.result: Limitations of the study include uncertainty about why AMP gene suppression in males does not lead to neurodegenerative phenotypes and the limited correlation between mRNA and protein levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C131 are explicitly acknowledged limitations by the authors. C130 identifies a gap in understanding the sex-specific effects of immune suppression. C131 is a general limitation of transcriptomic studies. These are appropriately recognized as areas requiring future investigation.

results.result: The study demonstrates that mild head trauma (vmHT) causes late-life neurodegenerative conditions that disproportionately affect females in a sexually dimorphic manner, with increasing age-at-injury exacerbating effects. The authors claim to establish a causal relationship between early head trauma and late-life neurodegeneration, with reproductive signaling adversely impacting female response.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm these core findings. Reviewer 1 states the work 'substantially advances our understanding of how sex-dependent response to TBI occurs,' Reviewer 2 notes 'the findings are interesting' regarding sex and age differences, and Reviewer 3 describes the results as 'compelling' and 'generally consistent and robust.' The evidence supporting conclusions is described as 'compelling with rigorous inclusion of controls and appropriate statistics.'

results.result: Sex peptide (SP) signaling is identified as a key factor in female susceptibility to post-injury brain deficits. Experiments with SP0 males and SPR knockdown (pan-neuronal and SPSN-specific) abolished injury-associated deficits in females, suggesting SP signaling through the reproductive pathway is responsible for vulnerability to injury-induced neurodegeneration.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently affirm this finding as a major contribution. Reviewer 1 states the work identifies 'the sex peptide and the immune system as modulators of sex differences,' Reviewer 2 notes they 'discover this is associated with exposure of the females to Sex Peptide,' and Reviewer 3 describes the identification of 'Sex Peptide as a modulator of greater negative outcomes in female flies' as demonstrating 'a novel signaling pathway.'

results.result: RNA sequencing reveals a reduction in innate immune defense transcripts (specifically Metchnikowin and Diptericin B) and increased Prophenoloxidase 2 expression specifically in mated females during late life (6 weeks post-injury). Seven unique genes altered in wildtype-mated female brains at the chronic timepoint may be involved in late-life neurodegeneration.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 expresses significant concern about the RNA-seq findings, stating 'it is also really surprising to see so few DEGs even in wild-type males and mated females and to see that none of DEGs overlap among groups or are even related to the SP-signaling.' They emphasize 'it is critical to independently verify their RNA-sequencing results and to add some more molecular evidence to support their conclusion.' Reviewer 2 notes the findings 'beyond Sex peptide are observational,' suggesting the evidence is insufficient for strong conclusions.

results.result: The vmHT paradigm had no significant effects on survival and produced age-dependent acute sensorimotor deficits. D3Inj flies showed no acute climbing deficits, D17Inj females showed transient deficits with recovery by 24hr, while D31Inj cohorts showed substantial and persistent deficits at 90min and 1 day post-injury.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as establishing the mild nature of the injury model. Reviewer 3 notes 'The authors have modified their previously reported TBI model in flies to mimic mild TBI, which is novel' and that 'Methods are explained in detail, allowing for reproducibility.' The characterization of the injury paradigm is not questioned by any reviewer.

results.result: At 1 day post-injury, vmHT did not generate changes in brain vacuolation, structural alterations in mushroom body or PDF neurons, or significant TUNEL staining. The authors conclude acute sensorimotor deficits were not caused by acute structural disruptions or neuronal death.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these acute findings. Reviewer 3 states 'Experiments are rigorous with appropriate statistics. A number of important controls are included.' The characterization of the mild injury as not causing immediate structural damage is accepted as supporting the model's validity.

results.result: Age-matched comparison at D45 shows vmHT decreased climbing index regardless of age-at-injury, with older ages inducing greater decline. Sensorimotor deficits were sexually dimorphic with females performing worse than males. Female flies showed significant increases in vacuolation for all age-at-injury cohorts, while males only showed increases in the D31Inj cohort.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently affirm these findings. Reviewer 2 states 'They find age and sex differences: older age is susceptible to mild TBI and females are also more susceptible.' Reviewer 3 notes the authors 'observe that increased age at the time of injury results in worse outcomes, especially in females.' The behavioral and pathological data are accepted without challenge.

results.result: Detailed movement analysis (mNGA) revealed vmHT caused shifts to slower speeds and aberrant climbing angles, with females showing deficits across all injury ages while males only showed changes in D17Inj and D31Inj cohorts. The impairments suggest disruption of both sensory and motor pathways.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question these detailed behavioral findings. Reviewer 3 notes 'The work tells a complete mechanistic story' and that experiments are 'rigorous with appropriate statistics,' implicitly accepting the movement analysis data as part of the comprehensive characterization.

results.result: Virgin females, despite being similar in size and mass to mated females, displayed little injury-induced climbing deficits and no significant changes in brain vacuolation at D45. The authors conclude that body size/mass differences are unlikely the cause of vulnerability, and that mating alters female biology to render it more vulnerable to neurodegeneration.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly affirm this finding. Reviewer 2 emphasizes 'they pursue a finding that virgin vs mated females show different responses: virgins are protected but mated females succumb to TBI with climbing deficits. In fact, virgin females compared to mated females are largely protected.' Reviewer 3 notes this demonstrates 'sex-dependent differences in recovery after TBI.' The virgin vs. mated comparison is accepted as a key result.

results.result: Post-injury mating experiments show that mating virgin females with wildtype males after injury reintroduced injury-induced phenotypes (increased vacuolation and decreased climbing), while mating with SP0 males did not. The authors conclude that pathways activated by SP signaling and vmHT interact and synergize to accelerate neurodegeneration.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as supporting the SP signaling mechanism. Reviewer 2 notes the authors 'discover this is associated with exposure of the females to Sex Peptide in the reproductive neurons of the female reproductive tract.' The post-injury mating experiments are not challenged and are viewed as part of the mechanistic story.

results.result: At the acute timepoint (1 day post-injury), D3Inj induced different numbers of transcriptomic changes in males (76 genes) versus wildtype-mated females (121 genes), with very few shared changes (14 genes), suggesting sexually dimorphic and reproductive status-dependent responses to vmHT.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 expresses concern about the RNA-seq findings, noting 'it is also really surprising to see so few DEGs' and that the authors should 'independently verify their RNA-sequencing results.' While the sexual dimorphism is noted, the small number of DEGs and lack of overlap raises questions about the robustness of the transcriptomic findings.

results.result: At the chronic timepoint (6 weeks post-injury), very small numbers of transcriptomic changes were observed across all conditions (males: 11 genes, wildtype-mated females: 8 genes, virgin females: 2 genes, SP0-mated females: 20 genes), with minimal overlap, suggesting sexually dimorphic and reproductive status-dependent chronic responses.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 specifically questions these findings, stating 'it is also really surprising to see so few DEGs even in wild-type males and mated females and to see that none of DEGs overlap among groups or are even related to the SP-signaling.' The request to 'independently verify their RNA-sequencing results' indicates uncertainty about the validity and interpretation of these chronic transcriptomic changes.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that injuries elicited very small numbers of differentially expressed genes across all conditions and timepoints, attributing this to the mild nature of the injury paradigm. They suggest mild injury may induce dynamic transcriptomic changes throughout the fly's lifespan and that not all flies may have experienced increased neurodegeneration.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 directly challenges the interpretation, stating 'The authors state that the reason is their TBI is very minor' but emphasizing 'it is critical to independently verify their RNA-sequencing results and to add some more molecular evidence to support their conclusion.' The authors' explanation for the small number of DEGs is not fully accepted by reviewers.

results.result: Background claims establishing that mild head trauma increases neurodegeneration risk, that establishing causative connections is challenging, and that Drosophila is an excellent model for studying neurodegeneration and TBI.
results.evaluation: These background claims are accepted without challenge by all reviewers. Reviewer 2 notes 'This is an interesting paper that allows a detailed comparison of sex and age in TBI which is largely only possible in such a simple model,' affirming the utility of the Drosophila model.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C19-C23 regarding acute injury effects. Both evaluations find the survival data and climbing index measurements well-supported with appropriate controls and statistics. OpenEval provides more technical detail about sample sizes, while peer reviewers accept these findings as establishing the mild TBI model.

Perfect agreement on claims C29-C34 regarding lack of acute structural damage. Both evaluations accept the imaging data across multiple modalities as demonstrating no immediate structural changes. Peer reviewers view this as supporting the validity of the mild injury model, while OpenEval notes the appropriate use of positive controls.

Strong agreement on claims C36-C42 regarding chronic behavioral deficits and age/sex differences. Both evaluations find the climbing index data and statistical analyses robust. Peer reviewers emphasize the age and sex susceptibility findings as major contributions, while OpenEval provides detailed assessment of the statistical methods.

Partial overlap on claims C43-C45 regarding chronic brain pathology. Both evaluations support these findings. OpenEval focuses on the quantitative imaging and spatial distribution analysis, while peer reviewers accept the pathological data as part of the comprehensive characterization of worse outcomes in females and older flies.

Perfect agreement on claims C56-C61 regarding detailed movement analysis. Both evaluations accept the idtracker.ai analysis as providing rigorous behavioral characterization. OpenEval notes the arbitrary definition of 'normal' climbing angle as a minor limitation, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the complete mechanistic story.

Strong agreement on claims C64-C68 regarding virgin vs. mated female differences. Both evaluations strongly support these findings. Peer reviewers emphasize this as a key result showing virgins are protected, while OpenEval notes the appropriate controls for body size differences and adequate sample sizes.

Strong agreement on claims C73-C76 regarding Sex Peptide signaling as a modulator. Both evaluations view this as a major contribution with strong evidence. OpenEval emphasizes the convergence of evidence from three independent genetic approaches, while peer reviewers describe this as identifying a novel signaling pathway.

Perfect agreement on claims C77-C79 regarding temporal SP exposure effects. Both evaluations support the post-injury mating rescue experiments. OpenEval notes the appropriate controls and sample sizes while acknowledging the mechanism remains unclear, and peer reviewers accept this as supporting the SP signaling mechanism.

Significant disagreement on claims C82-C86 regarding acute RNA-seq findings. OpenEval finds the data supported but questions the small number of DEGs and lack of overlap. Peer Reviewer 3 expresses stronger concern, finding it 'really surprising' and requesting independent verification, indicating uncertainty about the robustness of transcriptomic findings.

Significant disagreement on claims C87-C92 regarding chronic RNA-seq findings. OpenEval rates as supported but notes the surprisingly small number of DEGs raises questions about power and biological significance. Peer reviewers rate as uncertain and specifically question the lack of DEG overlap and request independent verification.

Significant disagreement on claims C93-C98 regarding immune-related genes. OpenEval finds the gene identification supported but notes the inference about neurodegeneration involvement (C98) is speculative without functional validation. Peer reviewers express stronger concern, with Reviewer 3 emphasizing the need for independent verification and more molecular evidence, rating as uncertain.

Agreement on uncertainty regarding claims C113-C116 about lack of persistent transcriptomic changes. OpenEval rates as uncertain, noting the explanations are speculative without direct evidence. Peer reviewers also rate as uncertain, with Reviewer 3 directly challenging the authors' explanation and requesting independent verification.

Partial disagreement on claims C118-C121 regarding immune gene dynamics. OpenEval finds the temporal dynamics supported by RNA-seq and literature but notes correlation does not establish causation. Peer reviewers express broader concern about the RNA-seq findings being observational and requiring more molecular evidence.

Strong agreement on claims C3-C8 representing main conclusions. Both evaluations affirm these core findings as well-supported. OpenEval notes 'causal' is a strong claim requiring additional validation, while peer reviewers describe the work as substantially advancing understanding with compelling evidence and rigorous controls.

OpenEval evaluates claims C51-C55 regarding recovery time-matched data as supported with appropriate controls. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these claims, though the overall experimental design is accepted by reviewers.

OpenEval evaluates claims C24-C25, C99-C102 regarding age-at-injury effects and consistency with human data as supported. No specific peer review evaluation addresses these claims separately, though peer reviewers accept the age-dependency findings as part of the broader results.

OpenEval evaluates claims C106-C109 regarding sex-specific age trajectories as supported but notes interpretations like 'plateau' are somewhat subjective. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these nuanced interpretations of the age-dependency data.

OpenEval rates claims C122-C129 regarding mechanistic model (Juvenile Hormone, immune homeostasis) as uncertain, noting they are largely speculative based on literature citations without direct experimental evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this mechanistic model.

OpenEval evaluates claims C31, C34, C49 regarding mechanisms underlying acute deficits as supported but notes these are inferences from negative results. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these mechanistic interpretations.

OpenEval evaluates claims C130-C131 as supported, noting these are explicitly acknowledged limitations by the authors. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these limitation statements.

Peer reviewers support claims C1-C2, C9-C15 regarding background and rationale for using Drosophila model. No corresponding OpenEval result specifically evaluates these background claims, though OpenEval implicitly accepts the model's validity through evaluation of experimental results.
